How does this make any sense when LED uses significantly less power?

Most LEDs require 3volt DC, the LED driver steps down the voltage from your 110 or 230 volt and rectifies AC to DC. Get that design wrong and your LED will probably work but have a monstrous lumens to energy consumption ratio that borders on conventional incandescent light bulb, even worse are drivers so poorly designed they have insane quiescent (off/inactive) current that borders on false advertisement.

LED lighting can be extremely efficient but only if every bit of it is designed that way.

Many LEDs (and other similar "energy-efficient" devices) work by drawing a large amount of power and lighting the LED at full power for just thousands of a second then it's off the rest of the time. The on/off timing determines how bright the LED will appear to the human eye. It happens at speeds faster than the eye can see, but the article is saying the meters don't make allowances for devices that have erratic power waveforms like that so you get meters registering way more power than is actually being used.

If you're a car enthusiast, you've probably seen that LED thing in videos without realizing it. You'll see newer tail-lights appear to be constantly blinking on and off in videos. That's because the LED "off" cycle matches the frames captured on the video.
